title: How Explainer Videos Support Accessibility and Inclusion (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: How Explainer Videos Support Accessibility
bullets: Deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision
slides.notes: An explainer video can reach people a slide deck misses, or it can shut them out. Here's how to make sure it brings more people in.

slides.title: Video spreads the load across channels
slides.notes: Text alone asks a lot of the reader. Video spreads the load across voice and image, and lets people pause, rewind and rewatch whenever they need.

slides.title: Video isn't automatically accessible
slides.notes: Missing captions, low contrast, colour-only signals and rushed pacing all shut people out. The good news is each one is fixable at the slide and script stage.

slides.title: Describe what matters on screen
bullets: Before: "As you can see, this one is much higher."
After: "Enrolments in the online course are higher..."
WCAG AA contrast, 24pt text or larger
slides.notes: Say what the chart actually shows, so blind and low-vision viewers can follow too. Then caption everything, check contrast and keep body text at 24 point or larger.

slides.title: One slide, made inclusive
bullets: Before: "Results", red, amber and green pie
After: "Most students passed the first assessment"
Direct labels: Passed, Resubmit, Not yet submitted
Offer a transcript or summary too
slides.notes: Swap a vague headline and colour-coded pie for a clear statement and labelled bars. Now the message works with sound or without, and with any colour vision.

slides.title: Turn accessible decks into explainer videos
bullets: Include captions, ask for a calm look
Try Basic first; Pro for a.i. direction
slides.notes: On Pro, a.i. directs the video, timing gentle animation to your narration so viewers follow by ear and eye. Try Basic first at powerpoint2vid.com.
